body: Irish licence plates are long and white on both front and back, with a blue EU strip on the left. This distinguishes them from UK plates, which have a yellow rear plate and often lack the blue strip.
Ireland uses yellow dashed outer lines on its roads, a feature not found in the UK. This is a key differentiator between the two countries.
Typical Irish architecture features cream-white buildings with black roofs, sometimes with grey corner stones. While British-style brick buildings exist, the white buildings are a strong clue.
Ireland is unique in Europe for its yellow diamond-shaped warning signs. Other types of signs, like regulatory signs, follow standard European conventions.
Many official signs in Ireland are bilingual, showing text in both English (regular font) and Irish (italic font).
Irish chevrons are yellow on black, which is a key difference from the UK's white-on-black chevrons.
Irish utility pole warning stickers feature a lightning bolt but lack the 'guy getting zapped' icon seen on UK stickers. They also often have a second rectangular sticker below the main one.
Irish yield signs say 'YIELD', whereas UK signs say 'GIVE WAY'.
Green and white bollards are a good clue for Ireland, especially when trying to distinguish it from the UK.
Rural Irish metal gates often have rounded corners, unlike the square-cornered gates common in most of the UK. Be aware that Northern Ireland also uses rounded-corner gates.
Small rural roads, known as 'boreens,' often have a strip of grass in the middle. This is a strong clue for Ireland in a 50/50 with the UK.
Ireland, like the UK, drives on the left side of the road.
Ireland's landscape is characterized by green agricultural fields divided by hedgerows. This is very similar to the landscape in many parts of the UK.
Both Ireland and the UK use wooden utility poles, often with thin metal rods as pole steps.
Double yellow lines on the side of the road indicate no-parking zones and are common in both Ireland and the UK.
Instead of diamond-shaped pedestrian signs, Ireland uses black and white posts with a yellow bulb (Belisha beacons), which are identical to those in the UK.
Ireland has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, recognizable by its lower position and large, sometimes transparent, circular blur with a small protrusion.

The first digit of 3-digit regional road numbers in Ireland indicates the general region, following an anti-clockwise pattern starting from Dublin. Roads starting with 8 or 9 are newer and less region-specific.
Irish phone numbers begin with a two-digit area code, and the first digit of this code corresponds to a specific geographical region.
The west coast of Ireland has a rugged, hilly landscape with wild moorlands and brownish grass, contrasting with the greener, neater fields of the east.
Small, hilly rural roads with Generation 4 coverage are a strong clue for the county of Donegal.
The Wicklow Mountains, south of Dublin, are hilly and look similar to the west coast, but you won't see the coast. Its small roads often have Generation 4 coverage.
A grey electric vehicle (EV) with a black semicircle on the back was used for much of the Generation 4 coverage in Eastern Ireland.
Distinctive tabletop mountains are a key feature of the landscape in northern Sligo and Leitrim counties.
The Burren National Park area is known for its unique karst landscape of exposed grey limestone rocks.
The city of Cork is notably more hilly than other major Irish cities.
